analysis.one_liner: Froze nearly all new federal rulemaking for two years, exempting only military and benefits-related rules.
analysis.headline: A bill to freeze essentially all new federal regulations until January 31, 2013, introduced by Sen. Mike Johanns with 10 Republican cosponsors, was referred to a Senate committee on September 8, 2011 and never received a vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have banned every federal agency from publishing new rules or finalizing, enforcing, or giving effect to draft rules until January 31, 2013 — a blanket 17-month moratorium covering health, safety, environmental, financial, and labor regulations. Rules for the military and foreign affairs, agency management, and benefits, loans, grants, and contracts were exempted. Introduced by Sen. Mike Johanns with 10 Republican cosponsors, it was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which took no action, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated industries — fossil-fuel and electric utilities facing air-pollution rules, manufacturers and chemical plants facing environmental and workplace-safety rules, and banks and other financial firms facing new Dodd-Frank rules — would gain roughly 17 months free of new federal requirements, plus the ability to keep challenging or lobbying against draft rules without facing an enforcement date. Businesses of all kinds would avoid compliance costs during a weak economy, and smaller firms facing new reporting rules would get temporary relief.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries facing new federal rules

how_it_helps.text: Would have prohibited any federal agency from publishing new rules or finalizing, enforcing, or giving lawful effect to draft rules until January 31, 2013, suspending compliance costs across the economy during the slow recovery from the recession.

The freeze applied not just to new rules but to draft rules already in the pipeline — including environmental and financial rules then under development — which industries could neither be forced to comply with nor have take final effect.

Exempted rules on military and foreign affairs, agency management and personnel, and public property, loans, grants, benefits, and contracts, so benefit programs and agency housekeeping could continue while substantive regulatory rules were frozen.

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the cost: worker-safety, clean-air and clean-water, food-safety, consumer, and financial-protection rules in development would be blocked from taking effect for 17 months, so hazards those rules address would go unaddressed. Workers, consumers, and communities near polluting facilities would absorb the resulting health, safety, and financial risks, while the government's normal system for weighing public comment on rules would be suspended.

drawbacks.text: The moratorium was indiscriminate: it would have blocked a rule protecting workers from a toxic exposure and a trivial paperwork rule in exactly the same way, delaying every health, safety, environmental, and financial protection pending in 2011 regardless of its merits.

Agencies would have had no way to respond to new hazards for 17 months — for example, a new contaminated-food outbreak, an emerging financial abuse, or a newly identified workplace danger could not be addressed by any binding rule.

Rules that had already gone through public comment and that businesses were counting on for clarity could not be finalized, leaving companies that had invested in the rulemaking process with continued uncertainty rather than relief.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — regulatory compliance relief during a weak economy — would have gone mainly to the industries subject to the rules, and some firms genuinely faced burdensome new requirements. But the bill's design was a blunt instrument: rather than reviewing or reforming specific costly rules, it shut down the entire federal rulemaking system, including protections against workplace, environmental, food, and financial harms, for nearly a year and a half. The costs would have fallen on people exposed to those harms, with no mechanism to distinguish a harmful rule from a necessary one.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee from the day it was introduced until the 112th Congress ended, and no committee or floor vote was ever held.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Johanns introduced the bill on September 8, 2011 with 10 Republican cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
The committee took no further action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or report to the floor appears in the action history.
The bill never received a vote in either chamber and expired when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, meaning the regulatory freeze it proposed never took effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public came out ahead in the narrow sense that the federal rulemaking system kept operating, so worker-safety, environmental, consumer, and financial rules in development could proceed to public comment and finalization. Industries that sought the freeze did not get it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public; the freeze never took effect

for.name: Sen. Mike Johanns
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Two-Year Regulatory Freeze Act and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: 10 of 47 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. McCain, Inhofe, Paul, Johnson of Wisconsin, Grassley, Thune, Barrasso, and Enzi.

against.name: Sen. Joseph Lieberman
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action; the bill stayed at referral with no hearing, markup, or report for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor, which remained the only route it could have taken since the committee did not report it.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 senators behind the bill — Johanns and 10 cosponsors — were Republicans, no Democrat joined, and because the bill never reached a floor vote there are no roll calls to confirm how the full chamber would have split.

industries.note: Utilities and fossil-fuel producers faced major EPA air-pollution rules in 2011–2012; the freeze would have blocked those rules from taking effect, shifting the cost of pollution onto public health. Because the bill never passed, they gained nothing.

A blanket moratorium would have suspended new environmental and workplace-safety requirements, saving compliance costs while leaving workers and nearby communities exposed to the hazards the rules address.
Agencies were writing Dodd-Frank rules at the time; freezing rulemaking would have postponed those consumer-protection and financial rules without touching the underlying law's obligations.
Many businesses would have gained relief from new compliance costs, but rules they had already shaped through public comment could not be finalized, prolonging uncertainty rather than resolving it.
